     1	# The base, worktrees seeded from its build, and the old code beside the new
     2	
     3	The base build is a clean worktree at the base, built once in place by ant. Every other worktree is seeded from it, with a copy of its build and caches. The old code is the base's code, run from the base build through `old-fortress.sh`, with a private caches folder.
     4	
     5	After the base build is built, run things in it only through `old-fortress.sh`. Any other run compiles into the caches that every worktree is seeded from.
     6	
     7	## Finding or building a base build
     8	
     9	- If your brief names a base build, use it. Earlier base builds are at paths such as `/home/user/fortress-base<N>`.
    10	- If not, look in `git worktree list`. A worktree can be your base build if it passes three checks:
    11	  - `git -C <it> rev-parse HEAD` prints your base;
    12	  - `git -C <it> status --porcelain` prints nothing;
    13	  - it holds `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`.
    14	- If no worktree qualifies, build one at a path of your own, outside the main tree. It takes about 200 s. Say so in your report.
    15	
    16	      git -C /home/user/fortress worktree add --detach <base-build> <base-commit>
    17	      cd <base-build>          # then set up the call as build-and-caches.md says
    18	      ant compileAll
    19	      # then the library order (build-and-caches.md), then this walk run, which warms walk's caches:
    20	      bin/fortress ProjectFortress/tests/BooleanOps.fss

     1	# The interpreter (walk)
     2	
     3	The code is in `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/`: `evaluator/` (the tree walker), `glue/` (the natives), `env/` and `rewrite/`. The library is `Library/` with `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`. The tests are in `ProjectFortress/tests/`, and `testSystem` runs them.
     4	
     5	## What walk does not do
     6	
     7	- Walk does no static checking. Its type-checking phase does nothing, and no switch turns it on. So every "type error" that walk prints is a dispatch failure at run time, and walk accepts programs that the specification forbids.
     8	- `fortress typecheck` checks against the compiler's prelude, so it says nothing about an interpreter program.
     9	- Walk chooses a coercion by the value at run time. The specification and the compiled path choose it statically. This is an accepted limit until the switch-over.
    10	- Walk's overload-ambiguity message names its two declarations in an order that varies from run to run. On one core the order is fixed for a given library, but a library edit can change it. Never compare or pin this order. The harness reads only that an `XXX` test fails.
    11	- `import java` is how the compiled path binds natives. Under walk, it is wired but unfinished, and no test uses it. Walk's natives are the `builtinPrimitive` strings (below).
    12	
    13	## Natives
    14	
    15	The library binds walk's natives by `builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.X")` strings in its `.fss` files. The classes are under `interpreter/glue/`. They take the evaluator's boxed values, so the compiled path cannot use them.
    16	
    17	A native can raise a Fortress exception that a Fortress `catch` sees. `Int.overflow()` in `interpreter/glue/prim/Int.java` does it like this:
    18	
    19	    throw new FortressError((FObject) Driver.getFortressLibrary().getRootValue(name));
    20	
    21	Walk wraps every other Java exception that a native throws in a `ProgramError`, so division by zero still ends the run.
    22	
    23	## Checks at load
    24	
    25	At load, walk checks the `comprises` clauses of the program's main component. It refuses a program with an extender that a clause does not allow. It does not yet check the library's clauses, another component's clauses or an object expression's clauses. To test such a refusal, name it with `load_exception_contains` in a `Name.test` file beside the program (`tests-writing.md`).
    26	
    27	## Running a program
    28	
    29	    bin/fortress P.fss
    30	
    31	- Walk searches for imports in the current directory first (`build-and-caches.md`, "Name resolution").
    32	- If `JAVA_FLAGS` is not set, `bin/fortress` uses `-Xmx256m -Xss32m`. Your setup gives a 4 GB heap, and the test harness uses 768 MB. A test can pass at two of these heaps and die at the third. If you claim that a run fails near a memory limit, measure the claim at 256 MB: run with `JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx256m -Xss32m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$PWD/tmp"`.
    33	- `FORTRESS_THREADS` sets the size of the work-stealing pool. Your setup sets 1. If it is unset, the pool has half the CPUs. A `for` loop is parallel unless every generator is `seq`. Walk evaluates the elements of a tuple and the operands of an operator in parallel.

    40	MicroGPT runs only under walk, by hand, never in the gate. `explorations/coordinator/tools/mg-run.sh <work-dir> <label> [threads]` runs its two checks at once: `explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlatCheck.fss` and `explorations/apl/mg/MicroGptAplCheck.fss`.      1	# The compiled checker, the code generator and the run-time
     2	
     3	The code is under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/`:
     4	
     5	- `scala_src/typechecker/`: the type checker, in Scala.
     6	- `compiler/`: the disambiguator, the desugarers, `phases/PhaseOrder.java`, overloading, `codegen/`, `NamingCzar` and `OverloadSet`.
     7	- `runtimeSystem/`: `InstantiatingClassloader`, tasks and transactions.
     8	- `compiler/runtimeValues/` and `nativeHelpers/`.
     9	
    10	The phases are parse, PREDISAMBIGUATEDESUGAR, DISAMBIGUATE, GRAMMAR, PRETYPECHECKDESUGAR, INTEGERLITERALFOLDING, TYPECHECK, DESUGAR, OVERLOADREWRITE and CODEGEN. The syntax tree is the only intermediate form. A switch of `Shell.java`, set for each command, decides which desugarings run; the phase list does not. The checker runs only on this path.
    11	
    12	The compiler does not compile every construct yet. For such a construct, the code generator calls `sayWhat` or throws another `CompilerError`: a code-generator wall.
    13	
    14	## What the code generator does
    15	
    16	- It makes every Fortress type a JVM reference type. For example, `RR64` becomes the run-time class `FRR64`. It emits no primitive `double` arithmetic.
    17	- It gives each overloaded name one dispatch method. The method tests the argument types from the most specific declaration to the least specific.
    18	- It compiles a generic declaration once, as a template. At the first load of each instantiation (`Box⟦RR64⟧`), `InstantiatingClassloader` makes the instantiation by rewriting the template's bytes with ASM.
    19	- The emitted classfiles stay at version 1.6, because this rewriting keeps no stack-map frames. Do not raise the version.
    20	- A size static argument is passed at run time as a descriptor from `RTTIsize.of`.
    21	- The `value` modifier has no effect on the representation.
    22	
    23	## The compiler's prelude, until the switch-over
    24	
    25	The compiled path uses the compiler's own prelude: `LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss`, `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss` and `Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss`. `Library/CompilerSystem.fss` is the compiled path's `System`.
    26	
    27	- Do not add a declaration to the three prelude files: they are deleted at the switch-over. Their tests stay.
    28	- The record does not yet say what happens to `CompilerSystem` at the switch-over.
    29	
    30	## Natives
    31	
    32	`import java com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.{...}` in a `.fss` file binds static Java methods over plain Java values.
    33	
    34	- The wrapper generator wraps every method of a class that it is given, the private methods too. If a type has no Fortress counterpart, it fails the whole import. So give every method of a helper class a signature that maps to Fortress, also a private method.
    35	- After you change a helper's signature, run the plain `ant compileAll`: with kept caches, the run links the old signature (`build-and-caches.md`).
    36	
    37	## Known shapes
    38	
    39	- The compiled path bounds an unbounded type parameter by `Object` before disambiguation; walk does not. This rejects every generic that is instantiated at a tuple type. The specification uses the bound `Any`. The difference stays until the switch-over.
    40	- An api and the component that implements it must have the same name. The linker looks for a component with the api's own name. If there is none, the link fails ("Could not find an implementation for API"), and the run dies with `NoClassDefFoundError`.
    41	- A failed compile of a program leaves a 0-byte jar in `bytecode_cache/`.
    42	
    43	## The `fortress` commands
    44	
    45	`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/Shell.java` dispatches `bin/fortress <command>`.
    46	
    47	- Regular use: walk, `compile`, `run`, and `junit X.test` for one compiled test by hand (`tests-running.md`).
    48	- To see what an early phase makes of a program, stop after that phase: `parse` (a syntax check), `disambiguate`, `grammar`, `desugar` or `typecheck`. `typecheck` checks against the compiler's own prelude, so it says nothing about an interpreter program.
    49	- `unparse` prints the syntax tree back as Fortress source. Use it to see what a desugaring made.
    50	- `link` links a compiled component (the `link` step of a compiled `.test` file). `api` writes a component's api. `test` runs a program's `test` declarations under walk.
    51	- The command chooses the library. Walk and `test` call `Shell.useInterpreterLibraries()`. Every other command calls `useCompilerLibraries()`. Each call points `WellKnownNames` and `Types` to its prelude, and sets the desugaring switches.
    52	
    53	## Running
    54	
    55	    cd ProjectFortress
    56	    # after any ant compileAll: the library order (build-and-caches.md)
    57	    ../bin/fortress compile <path>/P.fss
    58	    ../bin/fortress run P [args]
    59	
    60	A small program compiles in about 5 s and runs in about 1 s.
    61	
    62	## Before an edit
    63	
    64	Find where the fix belongs:
    65	
    66	- `explorations/coordinator/map/spec-to-implementation.md` gives each feature's parser rule, checker class, interpreter site, code-generator site and prelude location.
    67	- `explorations/coordinator/map/modules-and-phases.md` gives both pipelines, phase by phase.
    68

    73	- After a checker or code-generator edit, run your own tests through `junit.sh`. `tests-running.md`, "When to run a whole suite", says whether you run a whole track.

     1	# The library
     2	
     3	The library is `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`, without the compiler's own files there:
     4	
     5	- In `Library/`: the interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary.fss` and `.fsi`, and its other components. The compiler's `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerAlgebra` and `CompilerSystem` are not part of it.

    10	
    11	## The curator's decisions on the library
    12	
    13	Build on these decisions:
    14	
    15	- Exclusion (`excludes`, `comprises`) is used all over the library. The compiled checker keeps the multiple-instantiation exclusion rule.
    16	- The numeric tower is flat. The fixed widths, `ZZ`, `QQ`, `RR64` and `RR32` are siblings under `Number`, and each carries its own algebra. A wider type has a `coerce` from each narrower type. Walk converts by coercion at dispatch.

    16

    18	- It changes no line of the model program.
    19	- It changes no decision of the curator.

    21

    23	# Fortress: a briefing from memory
    24	
    25	Everything below comes from memory, with no sources checked. Each statement carries a tag: **[sure]**, **[likely]** or **[guess]**. Treat **[guess]** items as things to look up. Where the spec and the implementation disagree, the source tree is the authority. Large parts of the spec were never implemented, or were implemented only in part.
    26	
    27	---
    28	
    29	## 1. Why the language exists and what its designers aimed for
    30	
    31	- Guy Steele led the design in the Programming Language Research group at Sun Labs. **[sure]** Eric Allen, David Chase, Victor Luchangco, Jan-Willem Maessen and Sukyoung Ryu were core contributors, and Sam Tobin-Hochstadt was among the others involved at various points. **[likely]**
    32	- It began under DARPA's HPCS (High Productivity Computing Systems) program, alongside Cray's Chapel and IBM's X10. **[sure]** Sun was not funded for the program's final phase, around 2006, but kept the project going as open-source research. **[likely]**
    33	- Its slogan was "to do for Fortran what Java did for C." **[sure]** The name is often explained as a play on "secure Fortran." **[likely]**
    34	- The design goals were: **[sure]**
    35	  - Code that looks like mathematical notation, so a whiteboard formula and the program are nearly the same.
    36	  - Implicit parallelism by default, so the programmer must opt into sequential execution rather than into parallel execution.
    37	  - A "growable" language, in the spirit of Steele's *Growing a Language* talk. The core stays small, and most features (numbers, arrays, even many operators and reductions) live in libraries written in Fortress.
    38	  - A strong static type system with multiple inheritance of traits and symmetric multiple dispatch.
    39	- Version 1.0 of the specification appeared around 2008. **[likely]** Oracle acquired Sun in 2010. Steele announced in 2012 that active development was winding down. **[sure]** The stated reason was roughly that the hard remaining problems were implementing the type system (generic multiple dispatch with reified types) efficiently on the JVM, and that those problems were not worth more investment. **[likely]**
    40	
    41	## 2. The type system
    42	
    43	- **Traits** are the unit of inheritance. **[sure]**
    44	  - A trait may declare abstract and concrete methods, including bodies. **[sure]**
    45	  - A trait has no fields, though it can declare abstract getters. **[likely]**
    46	  - Multiple inheritance of traits is allowed: `trait T extends {A, B} ... end`. **[sure]**
    47	- **Objects** are the concrete, instantiable types. **[sure]**
    48	  - An object is a leaf. Nothing can extend an object. **[sure]**
    49	  - An object is either a singleton (`object Empty extends List end`) or parameterized by its fields, which also serve as the constructor: `object Cons[\T\](first: T, rest: List[\T\]) extends List[\T\] ... end`. **[sure]**
    50	  - Fields are immutable unless declared `var` or `settable`. **[likely]**
    51	- **Generic (static) parameters** are written `[\ ... \]` in ASCII and render as ⟦ ⟧ (white square brackets). **[sure]** The kinds are:
    52	  - Types (plain names, optionally with `extends` bounds). **[sure]**
    53	  - `nat n`, `int i` and `bool b`: compile-time values used in types such as fixed-size vectors and arrays. **[sure]**
    54	  - `opr ⊕`: an operator passed as a parameter. Algebraic traits such as `Monoid[\T, ⊕\]` use this to name *which* operation forms the monoid. **[sure]**
    55	  - `dim` and `unit`, for physical dimensions. **[likely]**
    56	  - Extra constraints go in `where { ... }` clauses. **[sure]** Where clauses can also introduce additional type variables, a form of bounded existential or hidden parameter. **[likely]**
    57	- **Variance:** generic types are invariant, and there is no declaration-site `+T` or `-T` as in Scala. **[likely]** Covariant-style APIs are approximated with extra type parameters and `where` constraints. **[guess]**
    58	- **Exclusion** has two forms. **[sure]**
    59	  - `excludes { U, V }` asserts that no type is a subtype of both.
    60	  - `comprises { A, B, C }` declares that every subtype of the trait is a subtype of one of the listed types. It is like Scala's `sealed`, but stated in the type. `comprises { ... }` with an ellipsis exists for hidden or private subtypes. **[likely]**
    61	  - Distinct object types exclude each other automatically, because objects are leaves. **[sure]**
    62	  - Exclusion exists mainly so the overloading checker can prove that two declarations never both apply (see §3). Without exclusion, many reasonable overload sets would be rejected as possibly ambiguous. **[sure]**
    63	- **Tuples, arrows and the top type** are structural and somewhat special.
    64	  - Arrow types are written `A -> B`, and a function can declare `throws`. **[sure]**
    65	  - `()` is the unit/void type. **[sure]**
    66	  - Tuple types are not ordinary trait types. I believe `Any` does not include tuples, so tuples cannot be stored as `Any` like an ordinary value. **[guess]**
    67	- **Contracts** can appear on declarations: `requires`, `ensures` and `invariant`. `property` declarations state algebraic laws, and `test` declarations are their checkable counterpart. **[likely]**
    68	
    69	## 3. Dispatch and overloading
    70	
    71	- Fortress uses symmetric multiple dispatch. A call chooses among overloaded declarations using the **run-time types of all arguments**, not just the receiver. **[sure]** It is close to Julia in spirit, unlike Java's static overloading.
    72	- **Compile time:** **[likely]**
    73	  - The static argument types determine the set of declarations that are applicable and accessible.
    74	  - The type checker assigns the call a static return type from the most specific *statically* applicable declaration.
    75	- **Run time:** among declarations applicable to the dynamic argument types, the most specific is chosen. **[sure]**
    76	- **Overload-set validity is checked statically, per pair of declarations**, so no run-time ambiguity can occur. **[sure]** For any two overloads of the same name, one of these must hold:
    77	  1. The parameter types exclude each other, so they can never both apply. **[sure]**
    78	  2. One declaration is strictly more specific than the other. **[sure]**
    79	  3. **The meet rule:** a third declaration exists whose parameter type is the intersection of the two, which resolves the overlap. **[sure]**
    80	- **Return-type rule:** if declaration A is more specific than B, then A's return type must be a subtype of B's. This keeps the static type sound under dynamic dispatch. **[sure]**
    81	- Making all of this modular with generics and multiple inheritance was a research problem in itself.     95	  - Statements in a `do ... end` block, separated by newlines or `;`.
    96	  - A sequential loop is written by wrapping the generator: `for i <- seq(1:n) do ... end`. **[sure]** There is also `while`. **[sure]**
    97	- **Generators** are `x <- expr`, where `expr` is a `Generator[\T\]` such as a range, array or set. **[sure]**

This is how parallel splitting becomes a library decision rather than a compiler decision. **[likely]** I believe the signature is roughly `generate[\R\](r: Reduction[\R\], body: T -> R): R`. **[guess]**
   100	- **`also`** creates explicit parallel blocks: `do A also do B also do C end`. **[sure]**
   101	- **`spawn e`** creates an explicit thread object. Its result is read with `.val()` or `.wait()`. **[likely]** The exact method names are **[guess]**.

   108	
   109	- **Two forms of the same program** **[sure]**
   110	  - Source is plain text, either ASCII or Unicode.

   113	  - You can type the Unicode characters directly instead. **[sure]**
   114	- **Rendering conventions:** **[likely]**
   115	  - All-caps or doubled-letter type names (`ZZ`, `RR`, `QQ`) render in blackboard bold.
   116	  - A trailing `_x` becomes a subscript.
   117	  - Identifiers in certain case styles render in italic, roman or bold.

   120	- **Declarations:** **[sure]**

   149	
   150	## 6. Numbers
   151	
   152	- **Integers** **[sure]**
   153	  - `ZZ32` and `ZZ64` (ℤ32, ℤ64) are fixed-width.
   154	  - `ZZ` is arbitrary precision. **[likely]**
   155	  - `NN32` and `NN64` are naturals. **[likely]**
   156	  - `IntLiteral` is the type of integer literals. **[likely]**

   158	  - `RR32` and `RR64` are floating point. **[sure]**
   159	  - `QQ` holds rationals. **[likely]**
   160	  - `CC` (complex) is in the spec, and the library implementation was partial. **[likely]**
   161	  - Interval arithmetic was mentioned in the spec. **[guess]**

   164	  - Digit grouping exists in the spec. I don't remember the separator. **[guess]**

   166	- **Coercion** **[likely]**
   167	  - Implicit conversions are user-definable through `coerce` declarations in the target type.
   168	  - The spec has detailed rules for resolving coercion against overloading, which essentially prefer no coercion to coercion.
   169	  - The interpreter implemented a subset of these rules. **[guess]**
   170	- **Dimensions and units** **[likely]**
   171	  - Physical dimensions and units were part of the type system in the spec: `dim Length`, `unit meter m`, values like `3 m/s`, and conversion with `in`.

   173	
   174	## 7. The standard library
   175	
   176	- **Library-first design:** much of the language is written in Fortress library code. **[sure]**
   177	  - The main files are `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin` (`.fsi` and `.fss`). **[likely]**
   178	  - Primitives call Java through a native or builtin-primitive mechanism, so many library operators bottom out in Java classes. **[likely]**
   179	- **Ranges** **[sure]**
   180	  - `a:b` is a closed range.
   181	  - `a#n` is a range that starts at `a` and has `n` elements.
   182	  - Strided and open forms exist.
   183	  - Ranges are generators.
   184	- **Arrays** **[likely]**
   185	  - `Array[\T, E\]` is the general type. `Array1`, `Array2` and `Array3` are specializations with static `nat` bounds and sizes.
   186	  - Vectors and matrices (`Vector[\T, n\]`, `Matrix[\T, m, n\]`) carry sizes in the type.
   187	  - Array literals use whitespace for columns and newlines or `;` for rows, as in `[1 2 3]`. **[likely]**
   188	  - Default indexing is 0-based. **[likely]** Indexing is `a[i]` and `a[i, j]`. **[sure]**
   189	  - Mutable and immutable arrays both exist.
   190	- **Collections** **[likely]**
   191	  - Lists, sets, maps and multisets exist as persistent or functional structures.
   192	  - Some are implemented as balanced trees with parallel generators.
   193	  - Strings were rope-like and built from concatenation nodes, so juxtaposition concatenation is cheap. **[guess]**
   194	- **Reductions and comprehensions** **[sure]**
   195	  - `SUM[i <- 1:n] a[i]` and `PROD[...]` are reductions.
   196	  - `BIG op [gen] body` reduces with any operator that has a big form. You declare one with `opr BIG ⊕ ...`. **[likely]**
   197	  - Comprehensions build collections: `{ x^2 | x <- S, x > 0 }`, `⟨ ... ⟩` for lists, and `[ ... ]` for arrays. **[likely]**
   198	- **The `Reduction` abstraction** has an empty element, a `join`, and possibly `lift` and `unlift`. Generators are parameterized over it, so one generator implementation serves all reductions. **[likely]**
   199	- **Algebraic traits** **[sure]**
   200	  - The library has a hierarchy parameterized by operator: `Associative[\T, ⊕\]`, `Commutative`, `Identity`, `Monoid[\T, ⊕\]`, `CommutativeMonoid`, `Group`, `Ring` and `Field`, plus ordering traits such as `PartialOrder` and `TotalOrder`. **[likely]**
   201	  - These traits are what make `BIG ⊕` reductions legitimately parallel. Associativity is *declared*, through `property` declarations, rather than proved. **[likely]**
   202	
   203	## 8. Components and APIs
   204	
   205	- **The two module kinds** **[sure]**
   206	  - An **API** (file extension `.fsi`) contains only declarations, like an interface for a module.
   207	  - A **component** (file extension `.fss`) contains implementations.
   208	  - A component `export`s one or more APIs and `import`s others: `import List.{...}`, `import Foo.{bar, baz}`, and `import api Foo`. **[likely]**
   209	  - A component's code may see only imported APIs, never other components directly. **[sure]**
   210	- **Linking** **[likely]**
   211	  - Components are linked into compound components by matching exports to imports.
   212	  - An `upgrade` operation replaces a component inside a compound one.
   213	  - The spec envisions a persistent, transactional "fortress" store that holds compiled components.
   214	- **The main program** exports `Executable` and defines `run()`. **[sure]** Early versions took `run(args: String...)`. **[guess]**
   215	- **Implementation** **[likely]**
   216	  - The interpreter implemented a simplified version: API and component files found on a path, one component per file, and imports resolved by name.
   217	  - The store and upgrade machinery were mostly not implemented.
   218	
   219	## 9. How the implementation was built
   220	
   221	- **Language and hosting** **[sure]**
   222	  - Everything was written in **Java**, and targeted the JVM.
   223	  - It was open source under a BSD-style license. It was hosted first on Sun infrastructure (sunsource.net / projectfortress) and later mirrored elsewhere. **[likely]**
   224	- **Front end** **[likely]**
   225	  - The parser was generated with **Rats!** (from Robert Grimm's xtc). It is a PEG/packrat parser, which suits whitespace-sensitive and extensible syntax.
   226	  - AST classes were generated from a declarative description by a tool called **ASTGen**. **[likely]**
   227	  - Some parts were written in Scala later in the project. **[likely]** I believe the type checker and some compiler phases were among them. **[guess]**
   228	- **Static phases** **[likely]**
   229	  - Disambiguation (names versus juxtaposition versus application), operator-precedence resolution, desugaring (generators, reductions and comprehensions into `generate` calls), and type checking with the overloading-validity checker.
   230	  - For long stretches, the interpreter ran with static type checking incomplete or off by default. Dispatch relied on dynamic checks. **[likely]**
   231	- **Interpreter** **[sure]**
   232	  - A tree-walking interpreter over the AST.
   233	  - Parallelism ran on fork/join work stealing. **[likely]**
   234	  - Run with something like `fortress run Foo.fss`. **[likely]**
   235	- **Compiler** **[likely]**
   236	  - Later work, around 2009 to 2012, compiled Fortress to **JVM bytecode** using ASM.
   237	  - It covered a subset of the language and specialized generics by instantiation, to work around erasure. **[guess]**
   238	  - The project ended before the compiler covered the whole language. **[likely]**
   239	- **Test suite:** a large directory of `.fss` test programs with expected output was used as the regression suite. **[likely]**
   240	
   241	## 10. The traps
   242	
   243	1. **Arguments, tuples and loops run in parallel.** **[sure]** `f(print "a", print "b")` has no defined order. A `for` loop that does `acc := acc + x` is a data race. Use `SUM`, a `BIG` reduction, `seq(...)` or `atomic`. Java habits will break things here.
   244	2. **Juxtaposition is not just function application.** **[sure]** Coming from Haskell, `f x` looks familiar, but `2 x` multiplies, `"a" "b"` concatenates, and the meaning depends on the left operand's type. Also, `f x y` does not curry as in Haskell. **[likely]**
   245	3. **Whitespace changes the parse.** **[sure]** `a -b`, `a[i]` versus `a [i]`, and unbalanced spacing around infix operators all matter. Scala and Java programmers assume whitespace is insignificant.
   246	4. **No global precedence table.** **[sure]** Parenthesize when mixing operators that are not conventionally related. Chained comparisons are conjunctions, not `(a < b) < c`.
   247	5. **Overloading is dynamic multiple dispatch.** **[sure]** This is unlike Java, where overloads are chosen statically. It is like Julia, but **the compiler statically rejects overload sets that could be ambiguous**, whereas Julia raises an ambiguity error only at run time. Expect to add meet declarations or `excludes` and `comprises` to get overload sets accepted.
   248	6. **Functional methods.** **[sure]** A method in a trait with `self` as a parameter is called as `f(x)`, not `x.f()`, and it overloads with top-level functions.
   249	7. **Objects are final and traits have no fields.** **[sure]** Scala users will look for class inheritance or abstract classes with state. There are none.
   250	8. **Generics are invariant**, with no Scala-style `+T` or `-T`. **[likely]** Type parameters are written `[\T\]`, not `[T]`, and `[...]` is indexing.
   251	9. **`=` binds and `:=` assigns.** **[sure]** `x = 5` is an immutable declaration, not an assignment. Writing it on an existing variable is a redeclaration or an error.
   252	10. **Evaluation is strict, not lazy.** **[sure]** Haskell's laziness and purity are absent. Mutation and effects are common, and laziness exists only inside generators by convention.
   253	11. **Fixed-width integers throw on overflow** instead of wrapping as in Java. **[likely]** Literals are not `int` or `Int`: they have literal types that coerce from context. **[likely]**
   254	12. **The spec and the implementation differ.** **[sure]** Dimensions and units, distributions and regions, full coercion rules, the component store and `upgrade` are in the spec but are absent or partial in the code. Check the tests and library source before trusting the spec.
   255	13. **The interpreter can be more permissive than the spec.** **[likely]** Code that runs under the interpreter may not pass the full type checker or the compiler. Don't treat "it runs" as "it's well typed."
   256	14. **The library defines the "language."** **[sure]** Many things that look built in, such as `+` on `ZZ32`, `SUM`, ranges and even some control-like constructs, live in `FortressLibrary`/`FortressBuiltin` and in Java primitives. Changing them means changing library code, and sometimes the Java primitive behind it, not the parser.

    66	
    67	Is the test suite shared between interpreter and compiler? No. Two hand-ported corpora: `tests/` shares no file name with `compiler_tests/`, and the 11 names it shares with `other_compiler_tests/` are different programs; only `parser_tests/` is read by both suites, and the gate's ladder stage also compiles and runs 82 files of `tests/`, each compared with its own earlier compiled output; nothing compares the two paths on one program (`test-coverage.md` B; FACTS § The harness and the gate).

    87	## 6. The development loop
    88	
    89	Measured (`test-coverage.md` D): `ant compileAll` about 80 s and it wipes the interpreter cache through `cleanCache`; `ant testFast` 5 min 23 s with the wall set by the indivisible `othercompiler` track; `ant testSystem` about 2 min in four shards; `ant testOnly -DtestPattern=X` 1 min 26 s for a one-second test, the cost being ant's fileset scan of `build/`; the 280 child JVMs of the `run` tests, at about 200 ms each, are not removable; every grammar-importing run leaves a 5.8 MB Rats! temp directory (`RatsUtil.java:138-144`), swept by `experiment/env.sh`.
    90	
    91	The two suites are therefore about nine minutes after a rebuild, before the gate's other stages, and neither test target compiles, so a stale `build/` silently tests the previous revision.
    92	
    93	Three loops, fastest first, are what the path needs.
    94	
    95	The shadow loop: compile one edited file with scalac or javac against the build classpath and put it first on the classpath; seconds instead of 80 s, no rebuild, no cache wipe, no tracked change. The template prototype ran its whole matrix this way; the recipe is in `perf-probes/template-check/run-all.sh` and `matrix.sh`. This is the loop for checker and code-generator edits.
    96	
    97	The program loop: a differential check that runs the three kernels and C4 on both paths and compares output, from `explorations/`; minutes. It is not built, since nothing microGPT-shaped compiles before the switch-over; it is the loop for phases 5 and 6 of `coordinator/PLAN.md`, and the only check that would say whether the target program still works.
    98	
    99	The gate loop: the gate of §0, run once on a batch's merged tree before any commit under the sealed tree lands on `main` (`coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md`). Running one JUnit class directly with `junit.textui.TestRunner` and the `fastTrack` macro's properties avoids the 86 s ant tax (the template worker's recipe, `perf-probes/template-check/`).
   100	
   101	Costs worth removing, in order of payoff: split the `othercompiler` track (the only structural gain left in `testFast`); decouple `compileAll` from `cleanCache` so a rebuild does not cold-start the next interpreter run; delete the Rats! temp directory at source (`RatsUtil`, already on the worklist as a one-liner); a direct-JUnit target in `build.xml` that skips the fileset scan. All four are `build.xml` or one-file edits, gated by the suite itself.

   103	Not a loop cost but a trap: the api cache key is the source directory path and staleness is by file date (`modules-and-phases.md` B.10), so a moved tree or a same-date edit gives a silent stale result; the shadow technique sidesteps it, editing under the sealed tree does not.

   115	calls one or the other per subcommand (`walk` vs `compile`/`run`/`link`).
   116	
   117	Consequences:
   118	- A `.fss` file is generally written for ONE world. `import java ...` means
   119	  compiler-only; `builtinPrimitive` means interpreter-only.
   120	- An *api name* used by both worlds is trouble: apis resolve by name along a
   121	  single shared source path (see below). This is exactly what broke the six
   122	  interpreter tests in the 2012 endgame (`api System` shadowed — see
   123	  test-baseline postscript) and why the compiler apis are `Compiler*`-prefixed.
   124	
   125	## The pipeline, phase by phase (verified 2026-09-08 from `compiler/phases/PhaseOrder.java` and `Shell.java`)
   126	
   127	Both execution paths share one phase list and differ only at the end. Parse (`parser/`, Rats!) produces the AST (`nodes/`); then PREDISAMBIGUATEDESUGAR, DISAMBIGUATE (names bound to declarations), GRAMMAR (syntax extensions), PRETYPECHECKDESUGAR, TYPECHECK (`scala_src/typechecker/`, writes a static type on every expression; no new representation), DESUGAR (comprehensions and big operators to `generate` calls with reduction objects, coercions, chained comparisons, getters/setters), then OVERLOADREWRITE and CODEGEN on the compiler path (`compilerPhaseOrder`, which also has INTEGERLITERALFOLDING before TYPECHECK) or OVERLOADREWRITE_FOR_INTERPRETER on the interpreter path (`interpreterPhaseOrder`). The AST is the only intermediate representation from parse to bytecode; there is no lower IR and no optimizing middle.
   128	
   129	The TYPECHECK phase is in the interpreter's list but is a no-op there: `walk` calls `setScala(false)` and the checking flag `fortress.compile.typecheck` defaults to false, and `StaticChecker` returns the tree untouched when off. `compile`/`build` set it on. Consequently the interpreter runs untyped desugared trees and accepts spec-illegal programs (e.g. `Value extends Number` against `Number comprises {RR64}`), and there is no command-line switch to enable checking for `walk`.
   130	
   131	What the code generator does with the static types: every Fortress type is lowered to a JVM reference type (traits to interfaces, objects to classes, `RR64` to the runtime class `FRR64` via `NamingCzar`; `CodeGen.java` emits no `DADD`), every overloaded name gets one generated dispatch method that tests argument types from most to least specific (symmetric multimethod dispatch on run-time types), and generic declarations are compiled once as templates whose instantiations (`Box⟦RR64⟧`, oxford brackets from `Naming.java`) are stamped out by `runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java` at first use by ASM rewriting of the template bytes; instantiation renames, it does not change representation. Emitted classfiles stay at version 1.6 because the load-time rewriting pipeline does not maintain stack-map frames and the JVM verifier may fall back to type inference only at that version. The `value` modifier on objects (spec: immutable fields, no identity) has no representation meaning in codegen.
   132	
   133	## Name resolution: fortress.source.path
   134	
   135	`default_repository/configuration` (overridable via `local_repository/`,
   136	`~/.fortress/`, `./.fortress/`, env vars, or `-D` flags) defines:
   137	
   138	    fortress.source.path=;.;${_fr}/LibraryBuiltin;${FORTRESS_AUTOHOME}/Library;${_fr}/test_library
   139	
   140	- Leading `;` sets the separator (Windows compat). `.` (cwd!) is searched
   141	  FIRST, then `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin`, then `Library/`.
   142	- `import Foo` finds the first `Foo.fsi`/`Foo.fss` on that path. First hit
   143	  wins — a file earlier on the path silently shadows a later one, and cwd can
   144	  shadow everything (mind where you run from).
   145	- The interpreter requires filename (sans suffix) == component/api name.
   146	
   147	## Cache anatomy and hygiene
   148	
   149	`default_repository/caches/` (gitignored by path, as is
   150	`ProjectFortress/test-caches/`; a cache written anywhere else, such as a
   151	probe's own `-Dfortress.caches` directory, is not ignored):
   152	- `analyzed_cache/`, `*parsed_cache/` — front-end analysis, shared-ish
   153	  between worlds; the main source of cross-world contamination.
   154	- `interpreter_cache/`, `environment_cache/` — interpreter side.
   155	- `bytecode_cache/` — compiler output: one jar per compiled component;
   156	  library components get api-qualified names (`fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`).
   157	- `nativewrapper_cache/` — generated wrappers for `import java` natives.
   158	
   159	Rules learned the hard way:
   160	- **Recompile what you edited; a wipe is not the fix.** Stale or order-inconsistent
   161	  caches produce *misleading* runtime errors
   162	  (`NoSuchMethodError: CompilerBuiltin.println(...)`,
   163	  `NoSuchMethodError: ...asJavaString()`, `Unable to read serialized data
   164	  ... recommend you delete the Fortress bytecode cache and relink`). These
   165	  are cache problems, not compiler bugs: recompile the component in the
   166	  library order (below), and run the library order after `ant compileAll`.
   167	- After editing a compiler-library `.fss` (`CompilerBuiltin`,
   168	  `CompilerLibrary` and the rest), `fortress compile` that component; the
   169	  interpreter's library (`FortressLibrary.fss` and the rest) needs nothing,
   170	  since walk re-reads it on its next run. What to recompile after each kind
   171	  of edit is the `fortress-repo` skill's `build-and-caches.md`.
   172	- **Compile order matters** on a fresh cache, because `fortress compile` of a
   173	  program does NOT emit the builtin-library jars, and the runtime classloader
   174	  then falls back to the **bootstrap stubs** in `ProjectFortress/build/fortress/`
   175	  (ant-compiled from checked-in `ProjectFortress/src/fortress/*.java` —
   176	  a *frozen, older* snapshot of CompilerBuiltin!). Symptom: NoSuchMethodError
   177	  on a method that plainly exists in CompilerBuiltin.fss. Recipe:
   178	
   179	      cd ProjectFortress
   180	      ../bin/fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/AnyType.fss
   181	      ../bin/fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss
   182	      ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerLibrary.fss
   183	      ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss
   184	      ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerSystem.fss
   185	      ../bin/fortress compile <program>.fss
   186	      ../bin/fortress run <component> [args...]
   187	
   188	  The JUnit harness gets this right because `CompilerJUTest` starts with
   189	  `Shell.resetRepository()` and compiles the world in dependency order.
   190	
   191	## Toolchain traps (JDK rungs)
   192	
   193	- **build.xml's javac tasks originally set `source=` but never `target=`**
   194	  (and three set neither). Harmless on JDK 8 (target defaulted to 8); on
   195	  JDK 11 target defaulted to 11 → v55 classfiles with invokedynamic string
   196	  concat → ASM 3.1's ClassReader (used by `ForeignJava.findClass` for every
   197	  `import java ...`) dies with `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`, failing all
   198	  compiler-path tests while testSystem stays green. Fixed by pinning
   199	  `target="${javaSourceVersion}"` on all 8 javac tasks (commit fdd4a57c2).
   200	  Diagnosis trick: a 20-line probe compiling against
   201	  `third_party/asm/asm-all-3.1.jar` + `javap -v | grep major` pinpoints
   202	  exactly which classfile ASM chokes on. (Surprise: JDK 11's *platform*
   203	  classes parse fine under `SKIP_DEBUG|SKIP_FRAMES|SKIP_CODE`; it was our
   204	  own freshly compiled v55 output that broke.)
   205	- `default_repository/caches/global.map`, the linker's state at the caches
   206	  root, is untracked and gitignored like the rest of the caches: the linker
   207	  writes an empty map wherever it is missing
   208	  (`linker/RepoState.java:366-385`), so `ant compileAll` or a wipe of
   209	  `default_repository/caches/*` needs no restore.
   210	
   211	## Generated code
   212	
   213	- Churn in the generated sources after a build is a regression to investigate,
   214	  never noise to revert.
   215	- AST nodes (`src/com/sun/fortress/nodes/`, 1000+ files),
   216	  `scala_src/nodes/FortressAst.scala`, `Library/FortressAst.fsi/fss` are all
   217	  generated by astgen from `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast` (build
   218	  target `makeAST`). They are checked in; ant's uptodate check compares
   219	  mtimes, so a fresh checkout looks current. If scalac errors show arity
   220	  mismatches in `S*Pattern` nodes: `touch ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast
   221	  && ant compileAll`.
   222	- Parser (`parser/*.java` from Rats! grammars), `precedence_resolver/
   223	  Operators.java` (from unicode data) — same pattern.
   224	
   225	## Test harness mechanics
   226	
   227	- Targets: `testFast` (unit + compiler suites, ~12 min, excludes interpreter
   228	  system tests), `testSystem` (interpreter, 382 tests, ~2 min),
   229	  `testLibrary`, `testCompiler`, `testNotPassing` (expected failures),
   230	  `testDemos`, nightly variants. Plain-text results land in
   231	  `ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS/TEST-<class>.txt`.
   232	- `.test` files (in `compiler_tests/` etc.) are property files driving
   233	  `FileTests`: keys like `compile`, `run`, `tests=`, `compile_err_equals=`
   234	  decide which phases run and what output to expect. `run`-tests execute the
   235	  compiled program via the `bin/run` script in a subprocess.
   236	- To reproduce one interpreter test: `../bin/fortress tests/<Name>.fss`
   237	  (from `ProjectFortress/`). Failures print the real diagnostic that the
   238	  JUnit boilerplate hides.
   239	- Suite runs reset/repopulate `default_repository/caches` — don't interleave
   240	  ad-hoc compiles with a running suite, and don't trust cache state after one.
   241	
   242	## Git archaeology techniques
   243	
   244	- **The history has a parallel root**: `5a68404` (David Chase, 2012-07-19,
   245	  4372 files) is a parentless import later merged by `575fe64`. Any
   246	  `git log <base>..HEAD -- <file>` therefore lists `5a68404` for almost
   247	  every file — useless for "who changed what since June". Use **content
   248	  comparison** instead: `git diff --quiet <base> HEAD -- <file>` and
   249	  `git show <base>:<file> | cmp - <other-tree>/<file>`.
   250	- The twelve pre-2016 branches are hg named-branch relics; the 2008 research
   251	  branches were squash-merged into trunk, so fine-grained authorship exists
   252	  only on the branch heads. Full survey with per-branch verdicts: see the
   253	  session notes / ask before deleting anything.
   254	- hg conversion quirks: empty "Starting/Closing branch X" marker commits;
   255	  `.hgignore` still in tree; David Chase's 2012-01-20 branch-closing sweep.
   256	
   257	## Environment gotchas (cloud container)
   258	
   259	- Current rung JDK 25 (`/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64`; 8/11/17/21 also
   260	  gated green); `unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` or the proxy's trust-store flags
   261	  pollute every JVM fork.
   262	- `web.archive.org` and `labs.oracle.com` are blocked by network policy —
   263	  research PDFs must be uploaded into the session by Pavol. Archived *pages*
   264	  (not PDFs) can be read via the pure.md relay; see the method note in
   265	  `research/extracts/fortress-websites-wayback.md`.
   266	- Gitignored files (e.g. `research/decks/*.pdf`) do not survive the
   267	  container; only commits and pushes persist.
